Servant of the LORD
SUR-vunt of the lord
noun
Hebrew Ebed Yahweh (H5650 + H3068) — "Servant of Yahweh"; the central figure of Isaiah's four "Servant Songs" (Isa 42:1-9; 49:1-13; 50:4-11; 52:13-53:12), the suffering Messiah who would bear the sins of many.

📖 Biblical Definition

Servant of the LORD is the central title of the four "Servant Songs" of Isaiah — Isa 42:1-9; 49:1-13; 50:4-11; and the climactic 52:13-53:12 — which together prophesy a coming Servant who would unite suffering, intercession, and exaltation in a way no OT figure ever had. The four songs progressively reveal: (1) the Servant's QUIET MINISTRY — "He shall not cry, nor lift up, nor cause his voice to be heard in the street" (Isa 42:2), the gentle non-coercive proclamation; (2) the Servant's COMMISSION TO ISRAEL AND THE GENTILES — "It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob...I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth" (Isa 49:6); (3) the Servant's OBEDIENCE UNDER SUFFERING — "I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting" (Isa 50:6); and most weighty, (4) the SUBSTITUTIONARY ATONEMENT — "He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed" (Isa 53:5). Isaiah 53 is the great prophetic chapter of substitutionary atonement, quoted by Christ Himself ("he was reckoned among the transgressors," Luke 22:37) and applied to Christ by the early church (Acts 8:32-35 — Philip and the Ethiopian eunuch; 1 Pet 2:21-25). The title "Servant" is also Christ's self-designation: "the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many" (Mark 10:45). The greatest title in the universe (Lord) is held by the One who took the lowest position (Servant) — and through Servant-obedience He was exalted to the highest Name (Phil 2:5-11).

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The central figure of Isaiah's four Servant Songs; the suffering Messiah who bears the sins of many; the title Christ applied to His own ministry.

SERVANT OF THE LORD, noun. The central figure of Isaiah's four Servant Songs: Isa 42:1-9; 49:1-13; 50:4-11; 52:13-53:12. Hebrew Ebed Yahweh.

Climactic in Isaiah 53 — the great prophetic chapter of substitutionary atonement ("He was wounded for our transgressions"). Fulfilled in Christ (Acts 8:32-35; 1 Pet 2:21-25; Mark 10:45).

📖 Key Scripture

Isaiah 53:4-5 — "Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed."

Isaiah 49:6 — "And he said, It is a light thing that thou shouldest be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob, and to restore the preserved of Israel: I will also give thee for a light to the Gentiles, that thou mayest be my salvation unto the end of the earth."

Mark 10:45 — "For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many."

Philippians 2:7-9 — "But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Servant of the LORD is corrupted when Isaiah 53 is reduced to mere prophetic poetry about Israel's national suffering (collective-Israel-as-servant reading), or when the substitutionary-atonement doctrine of "bruised for our iniquities" is softened into example-only theology (Christ shows us how to suffer, but doesn't substitute for us).

expand to see more

Collective-Israel reading. Modern Jewish (and some modernist Christian) interpretation reads the Servant of Isaiah 53 as Israel collectively — the suffering nation as the Servant who bears the world's pains. But the New Testament treats it as INDIVIDUAL Messianic prophecy: the Ethiopian eunuch reads Isa 53 and asks Philip "of whom speaketh the prophet this? of himself, or of some other man?" Philip's answer (Acts 8:35): he "preached unto him Jesus." Peter quotes Isa 53 about Christ's atonement (1 Pet 2:24-25). The canonical interpretation is individual-Messianic; collective-Israel readings are post-NT attempts to deflect the messianic claim.

Example-only atonement. Liberal theology often reduces "he was wounded for our transgressions" to Christ-as-moral-example: he showed us how to suffer nobly. But Isaiah 53 is explicit about substitution: "the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all" (53:6); "by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities" (53:11); "he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many" (53:12). The pile-up of substitutionary language is unmistakable: he TOOK what was OURS. Example theology removes the gospel by leaving us still bearing our own sin.
